First-time home buyers’ GST rebate on a new home: up to CAD 50,000 back, a 15% marginal tax between CAD 1 million and 1.5 million, and what an upgrade really costs

Work out the GST (or federal part of the HST) still payable on a new home bought from a builder after the first-time home buyers’ rebate and the new housing rebate, why each extra dollar of price costs 15 cents of federal tax inside the CAD 1 million to 1.5 million phase-out, how the five-year look-back decides who is a first-time buyer, and what the PBO projects for the number of rebates.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 9 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Price the first-time home buyers’ GST rebate on a new home: the rebate, the GST still payable, and what an upgrade costs inside the CAD 1 million to 1.5 million phase-out

Interactive planning lab

GST or federal part of the HST on the price$55,000
First-time home buyers’ rebate$40,000
New housing rebate$0
GST still payable after rebates$15,000
Extra GST payable on the added $50,000$7,500
Extra monthly mortgage payment for the added price and GST$289.92

At $1,100,000 the GST or federal part of the HST is $55,000. As a first-time buyer you get back $40,000 and pay $15,000. Because the price is inside the CAD 1 million to 1.5 million phase-out, each extra dollar of price costs about 15 cents of federal tax, not 5: adding $50,000 raises the GST payable by $7,500, so the change costs $57,500 and about $290 a month on the mortgage.

The central idea

A first-time buyer who signs an agreement with a builder after 19 March 2025 and before 2031 gets back all of the GST, or the federal part of the HST, on a new home priced up to CAD 1 million, to a maximum of CAD 50,000. Between CAD 1 million and 1.5 million the rebate falls in a straight line to nil, so each extra dollar of price adds 5 cents of tax and removes 10 cents of rebate: a 15% marginal rate. A CAD 50,000 upgrade on a CAD 1.1 million home therefore costs CAD 57,500. First-time status is tested on the day ownership is transferred, with a look-back over that calendar year and the four before it. The PBO projects about 12,900 rebates for homes completed in 2026.

01

Why the price of a new home matters twice

A newly built home is taxable: the builder charges GST, or HST in the participating provinces, on the price. For decades the main relief has been the GST/HST new housing rebate, which returns at most CAD 6,300 and disappears at a price of CAD 450,000. Since 2025 there is a much larger rebate for first-time buyers: up to CAD 50,000, enough to cancel all of the federal tax on a home priced up to CAD 1 million.

The size of that rebate depends on the price. Above CAD 1 million it shrinks, which changes the arithmetic of every decision that moves the price: a bigger unit, a parking spot, an upgrade package, a price escalation clause. The calculator answers three questions for a home bought from a builder: how much GST or federal HST is still payable after the rebates, what an addition to the price costs once the rebate shrinks, and what that does to the mortgage payment.

02

The rule in the Excise Tax Act and CRA’s worksheet

The rebate is in subsection 254(2.1) of the Excise Tax Act. For a home bought from a builder, CRA’s Form RC7190-WS works it out in three lines: line 12 is the GST, or the federal part of the HST, paid; line 13 is the price before tax; line 14 is the rebate.

Price before tax (line 13)First-time buyers’ amount (line 14)New housing rebate, any eligible buyer
CAD 350,000 or lessAll of the GST paid36% of the GST (full, at most CAD 6,300)
Over CAD 350,000, under CAD 450,000All of the GST paidPhased out: × (450,000 − price) ÷ 100,000
CAD 450,000 to 1,000,000All of the GST paid, at most CAD 50,000Nil
Over CAD 1,000,000, under CAD 1,500,000Lesser of CAD 50,000 and the GST, × (1,500,000 − price) ÷ 500,000Nil
CAD 1,500,000 or moreNilNil

Up to CAD 1 million the Act sets the first-time buyers’ rebate at the lesser of CAD 50,000 and the tax paid, less the new housing rebate, and pays it in addition to that rebate, so together they return the lesser of the two. The calculator shows the two parts separately. At 5% GST, CAD 50,000 is exactly the tax on CAD 1 million, so the cap and the start of the phase-out meet.

The HST is handled by converting to the federal part: CRA’s worksheet multiplies the HST by 5/13, 5/14 or 5/15. In Ontario, HST of CAD 143,000 on a CAD 1.1 million home contains CAD 55,000 of federal tax. This rebate applies only to that CAD 55,000. Any provincial rebate is a separate claim; RC4028 notes, for example, that the Ontario new housing rebate (at most CAD 24,000) can be available above the federal thresholds.

03

Who is a first-time buyer, and when it is tested

According to CRA’s guide RC4028, the buyer generally must be at least 18, a Canadian citizen or permanent resident, and must not have lived, as their primary place of residence, in a home that they or their spouse or common-law partner owned, in the current calendar year or the four before it, anywhere in the world. The other conditions for a home bought from a builder are:

  • the agreement of purchase and sale was entered into after 19 March 2025 and before 2031;
  • construction begins before 2031 and is substantially completed before 2036, and ownership is transferred before 2036;
  • the home is bought as the buyer’s primary place of residence, and the buyer is the first individual to occupy it after completion;
  • the buyer has never received the rebate before. It is once per lifetime.

The first-time test applies at the moment ownership is transferred, not when the agreement is signed. For a pre-construction condominium that can be years later, often after a period of interim occupancy. A buyer who signs in 2026, then buys and moves into a resale home while waiting, has lived in an owned home in the look-back window by the time the condominium is transferred. A partner’s ownership counts too: moving into a spouse’s owned home is enough.

Only one person can claim per home. When two people buy together, at least one must be a first-time buyer who will live there; that person is the claimant. A corporation or partnership cannot claim. RC4028 also excludes an agreement made before 20 March 2025 that is later varied, amended or assigned, and a cancelled-and-replaced agreement where obtaining the rebate was the main reason.

04

The 15% band: what the next dollar of price costs

Between CAD 1 million and 1.5 million the GST still payable by a first-time buyer is 5% of the price less a rebate that falls by CAD 50,000 over CAD 500,000, or 10 cents per dollar. The GST payable therefore rises by 15 cents for every extra dollar of price, from nil at CAD 1 million to CAD 75,000 at CAD 1.5 million. Above CAD 1.5 million the rate falls back to the statutory 5%.

CAD 400,000CAD 20,000CAD 20,000CAD 0CAD 16,850
CAD 600,000CAD 30,000CAD 30,000CAD 0CAD 30,000
CAD 1,000,000CAD 50,000CAD 50,000CAD 0CAD 50,000
CAD 1,100,000CAD 55,000CAD 40,000CAD 15,000CAD 55,000

CAD 1,400,000CAD 70,000CAD 10,000CAD 60,000CAD 70,000
CAD 1,500,000CAD 75,000CAD 0CAD 75,000CAD 75,000

Other buyers face their own, smaller notch: the new housing rebate makes their rate 3.2% below CAD 350,000 and 11.3% between CAD 350,000 and 450,000, where CAD 6,300 of rebate is lost over CAD 100,000.

05

Five worked cases

The calculator’s default is a first-time buyer, never an owner, buying a CAD 1.1 million home from a builder with a CAD 220,000 down payment and a 30-year mortgage at 4.5% compounded half-yearly, and considering CAD 50,000 of upgrades.

  1. The base price. GST is CAD 55,000. The rebate is CAD 50,000 × (1,500,000 − 1,100,000) ÷ 500,000 = CAD 40,000, leaving CAD 15,000 payable. If that is financed, the mortgage is CAD 895,000 and the monthly payment about CAD 4,513.
  2. Adding CAD 50,000 of upgrades. At CAD 1.15 million the GST is CAD 57,500 and the rebate CAD 35,000, so the GST payable rises by CAD 7,500, three times the CAD 2,500 that 5% would suggest. The upgrade costs CAD 57,500 in all and adds about CAD 290 a month to the payment.
  3. The same CAD 50,000 at other prices. From CAD 900,000 or CAD 950,000 it adds no GST, because the total stays within CAD 1 million. From CAD 1 million, or from CAD 1.45 million up to exactly CAD 1.5 million, it adds CAD 7,500. From CAD 1.5 million it adds CAD 2,500.
  4. Not a first-time buyer. Someone who lived in a home they owned three years ago gets no first-time rebate, and no new housing rebate at this price: the full CAD 55,000 is payable, CAD 40,000 more than the first-time buyer.
  5. A CAD 450,000 condominium. GST is CAD 22,500 and the first-time buyer gets all of it back. Any other buyer gets nothing, because the new housing rebate ends at CAD 450,000.

An independent 40-digit decimal check reproduces every figure above, and the tests check that the rebate never exceeds CAD 50,000, never exceeds the GST, and that the GST payable never falls as the price rises.

06

What the Parliamentary Budget Officer projects

No count of rebates claimed has been published yet. The Parliamentary Budget Officer’s June 2025 costing (RP-2526-001-S) built its estimate from projected housing completions and narrowed them step by step. The figures are projections, not observations:

Step20262025 to 2030
Houses and apartments completed237,3241,482,406
Intended for the ownership, condominium and co-op markets137,956835,884
Bought as a primary residence by citizens and permanent residents67,329407,948
Bought by first-time buyers13,39381,146
Valued under CAD 1.5 million12,90377,253
Bought after the effective date (rebate paid)12,90371,711

The PBO projected 71,711 rebates averaging CAD 26,832, a cost of about CAD 1.9 billion over six years, covering 4.8% of projected completions. Its first-time share, about 20% of qualifying sales, came from Statistics Canada’s Canadian Housing Statistics Program data for three provinces. It assumed agreements after 26 May 2025, the date in the bill at the time; the law as enacted reaches back to 20 March 2025, so the 2025 figure is likely understated.

07

Before you sign, and before closing

  1. Check the look-back for both partners against the expected transfer year, not the signing year. A resale purchase while waiting for a new build can end eligibility.
  2. Inside the CAD 1 million to 1.5 million band, every dollar added to the price costs CAD 1.15. Upgrades, parking, a storage locker and escalation clauses bought from the builder raise the price; in the calculator, add them to the price to see the GST that follows. An assignment price paid to a previous buyer is also part of the price on line 13.
  3. Ask whether the builder will pay or credit the rebate. RC4028 allows the builder to credit the new housing rebate and the first-time buyers’ rebate against the amount due at closing (Form GST190, Type 1A, sent by the builder). If the builder does not, apply to CRA yourself (Type 2); for a home bought from a builder this is generally within two years after ownership is transferred.
  4. Keep the cash plan separate. A rebate credited at closing reduces the amount owing; one claimed later is cash that arrives after the down payment, land transfer tax and closing costs have been paid.

08

What the calculator leaves out

  • Provincial tax. Only the federal 5% is modelled. In the HST provinces the provincial part, and any provincial rebate, are not shown.
  • Other ways to buy. Owner-built homes, co-op shares, and homes on leased land (Types 1B, 3 and 5 on the worksheet) use different price thresholds and are not modelled.
  • Eligibility dates. The calculator checks age, status and the look-back only. It does not check the agreement date, construction dates or whether you will be the first occupant.
  • Closing costs and insurance. Land transfer tax, legal fees and adjustments are left out. A down payment under 20% needs mortgage default insurance, whose premium and price limits are not applied; amortization is entered, not checked against lender rules.
  • Mortgage terms. The payment uses a fixed rate for the whole amortization, compounded half-yearly as for Canadian fixed-rate mortgages.
